A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same SEMA research work. Their main text, equations, figures, tables and complete appendices are readable and support reliable comparison across renumbering and relocation.

before.justification: V1 reports original ImageNet-1K classification, higher-resolution fine-tuning, COCO segmentation and averaging-ablation results.

after.justification: V2 retains original experiments and adds ADE20K segmentation, runtime measurements, resolution-generalization tests and ablations. Appendix C separately identifies its medical-image results as reproduced from Dayag et al.

M1.justification: The core window-attention-plus-averaging design and value projection remain. However, v1 Algorithm 2 applies RoPE to Qw, Kw and Vw, whereas v2 Appendix G applies it only to Qw and Kw. This changes the specified procedure; the PDFs do not establish whether the implementation changed or its description was corrected.

E1.justification: V2 adds ADE20K semantic segmentation and evaluates models trained at 224 squared on larger-resolution inputs without fine-tuning, introducing a resolution-shift scenario. Appendix C also presents medical segmentation benchmarks, but explicitly as results reproduced from another work rather than new SEMA experiments.

E2.justification: Within ImageNet Table 2, v2 adds Flatten-CSwin-T and removes EfficientFormerV2-L and LRFormer-S. It also reports larger baseline variants and introduces ResNet-50 and DeiT-S + MLN in the ADE20K comparison. The principal comparator families remain; DefMamba-S matches v1's DefMamba entry rather than constituting a new tiny-scale comparator.

E3.justification: Evaluation expands from tiny models to T/S/B configurations, adds untuned resolution testing, extends classification to 1024 squared and measures latency through 2048 squared. ADE20K introduces single-scale and multi-scale mIoU evaluation. The stated ImageNet initial learning rate is corrected from 4×10^3 to 4×10^-3; this textual correction does not establish that retained experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: V2 retains the original averaging ablation but adds a value-projection removal control and averaging ablations at 672 squared with and without fine-tuning (Tables 7–8). It also adds untuned resolution-robustness tests and quantitative analysis of pretrained MILA's dispersion coefficients. These substantially broaden investigation of which components help and under what conditions.

E5.justification: V2 newly discloses that most experiments use one run and that SEMA-T was consistent across an unspecified several runs. Runtime results average 1000 executions, and the dispersion analysis reports distribution means and standard deviations. Accuracy confidence intervals, exact repeat counts and seeds remain unspecified; an increase in training repetitions is not established.

E6.justification: V2 adds SEMA-S/B ImageNet accuracies of 84.6/85.4, ADE20K mIoU of 48.2/48.5, and new runtime, untuned-resolution, ablation and dispersion results. SEMA-T's 83.7 accuracy, previously reported fine-tuned accuracies and COCO AP values remain unchanged. Table 2 drops MILA-T's published 83.5 entry while retaining 83.3 without v1's retraining marker; SEMA's COCO FLOPs change from 277G to 275G.

T1.justification: V2 adds Proposition 3.5/B.4, a probabilistic dispersion statement under bounded covariance and sparse positive dependence, with a new proof. It revises the generalized-attention definition and deterministic proof, explicitly handling all queries and heads, and corrects attention formulas and the Mamba induction. V1's auxiliary dispersion lemma is incorporated into the revised proof rather than substantively discarded.

C1.justification: The abstract and introductory contributions retain the same central dispersion, localization, averaging and scalability claims. The conclusion extends the claimed theoretical grounding to both deterministic and probabilistic analysis and explicitly claims robustness, supported by the newly presented resolution-transfer experiments.

C2.justification: V1 treats the 0.2-point averaging gain mainly as support for its design. V2 explains that value projection contributes more at standard resolution, while averaging matters increasingly at larger resolutions, and discusses how fine-tuning may alter dispersion. It also interprets measured dispersion differences between vision and language and sharpens limitations: practical token counts may not approach the asymptotic regime, and demonstrated applicability remains limited to vision.

D1.justification: V2 adds a source-code link and a supplemental-code statement, ADE20K implementation and optimizer settings, SEMA-S stage depths, and the batch size for 1024-squared inputs. Appendix D newly documents higher-resolution window size and distinct VMamba/SEMA fine-tuning recipes. These substantially expand reproducibility information without establishing that retained experiments changed.

R1.justification: V2 adds connections to multi-query attention and DeepSeek-V2 latent attention, discusses the cited USEMA medical adaptation, and adds references supporting new experiments and probability analysis. It removes references associated with CPE, EfficientFormerV2 and LRFormer. The central positioning relative to MILA, Swin and earlier dispersion research remains substantially unchanged.

P1.justification: The experimental narrative is reorganized into task-specific discussions, the brief appendix ablation becomes an expanded main-text Section 6, and limitations move to Appendix A. Algorithms and MILA justification move into appendices, alongside new experiment-setting sections. This substantially changes document organization even though much introductory and related-work prose is retained.

P2.justification: V2 adopts a two-column main text and extensively restructures displays: ImageNet comparisons are grouped by model scale, Table 3 gains untuned results, and COCO's vertically stacked panels become side-by-side columns. New runtime, segmentation and ablation tables are added. Existing diagrams are retained and resized or relocated, while the paired main-text algorithms become one appendix algorithm.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially strengthens validation of SEMA's central design: Tables 7–8 separate value-projection and averaging effects, Table 3 tests resolution transfer without retraining, and Tables 4 and 6 add measured speed and semantic-segmentation evidence. Expanded implementation details and code-access information improve reproducibility. These gains outweigh reporting weaknesses, including mostly single-run accuracy results and the new probabilistic proof's failure to justify its stated simultaneous guarantee over all sufficiently large sequence lengths.
